nodes.label: Continue linear sequences
nodes.description: Determine the common difference of a sequence by subtracting successive terms, and use it to write down the next terms of a linear sequence, including the next picture in a figure pattern.

nodes.label: Identify terms using T_n
nodes.description: Use the T_n notation to identify the term at a given position (such as T_6, T_{n-1} or the first three terms), distinguishing the position n from the value T_n, including for a repeating pattern of letters.

nodes.label: Find the general formula
nodes.description: Find the general formula T_n = dn + c for a linear sequence from a table, a list of terms or a picture pattern.

nodes.label: Use the general formula
nodes.description: Use the general formula T_n to calculate a required term (such as the missing terms or T_25) and to solve for n when the value of a term is given.

nodes.label: Unknowns in linear sequences
nodes.description: Determine the common difference of a sequence whose terms contain an unknown, find the value of the unknown that makes the terms a linear sequence, and evaluate the terms.

content.text_md: You and $\text{3}$ friends decide to study for Maths and are sitting together at a square table. A few minutes later, $\text{2}$ other friends arrive and would like to sit at your table. You move another table next to yours so that $\text{6}$ people can sit at the table. Another $\text{2}$ friends also want to join your group, so you take a third table and add it to the existing tables. Now $\text{8}$ people can sit together. Examine how the number of people sitting is related to the number of tables. Is there a pattern? [figure] Two more people can be seated for each table added.

Make a table to see if a pattern forms: Number of tables, n Number of people seated $\text{1}$ $4=4$ $\text{2}$ $4+2=6$ $\text{3}$ $4+2+2=8$ $\text{4}$ $4+2+2+2=10$ $\vdots$ $\vdots$ n $4+2+2+2+\cdots+2$

Describe the pattern: We can see that for $\text{3}$ tables we can seat $\text{8}$ people, for $\text{4}$ tables we can seat $\text{10}$ people and so on. We started out with $\text{4}$ people and added two each time. So for each table added, the number of people increased by $\text{2}$ . So the pattern formed is $4;6;8;10;\ldots$ .

As before, you and $\text{3}$ friends are studying for Maths and are sitting together at a square table. A few minutes later $\text{2}$ other friends arrive so you move another table next to yours. Now $\text{6}$ people can sit at the table. Another $\text{2}$ friends also join your group, so you take a third table and add it to the existing tables. Now $\text{8}$ people can sit together as shown below. Find an expression for the number of people seated at $n$ tables. Use the general formula to determine how many people can sit around $\text{12}$ tables. How many tables are needed to seat $\text{20}$ people? [figure] Two more people can be seated for each table added.

Make a table to see the pattern: Number of Tables, $n$ Number of people seated Pattern $\text{1}$ $4=4$ $=4+2\left(0\right)$ $\text{2}$ $4+2=6$ $=4+2\left(1\right)$ $\text{3}$ $4+2+2=8$ $=4+2\left(2\right)$ $\text{4}$ $4+2+2+2=10$ $=4+2\left(3\right)$ $\vdots$ $\vdots$ $\vdots$ n $4+2+2+2+\cdots+2$ $=4+2\left(n-1\right)$ Note: There may be variations in how you think of the pattern in this problem. For example, you may view this problem as the person on one end fixed, two people seated opposite each other per table and one person at the other end fixed. This results in $1+2n+1=2n+2$ . Your formula for $T_n$ will still be correct.
Describe the pattern: The number of people seated at $n$ tables is ${T}_{n}=4+2\left(n-1\right)$

Calculate the term, in other words, find if: $\begin{aligned}T_{12}&=4+2\left(12-1\right)\\&=4+2\left(11\right)\\&=4+22\\&=26\end{aligned}$ Therefore $\text{26}$ people can be seated at $\text{12}$ tables.

Calculate the number of tables needed to seat people, in other words, find if: $\begin{aligned}T_{n}&=4+2\left(n-1\right)\\20&=4+2\left(n-1\right)\\20&=4+2n-2\\20-4+2&=2n\\18&=2n\\\frac{18}{2}&=n\\n&=9\end{aligned}$ Therefore $\text{9}$ tables are needed to seat $\text{20}$ people.

Raymond subscribes to a limited data plan from Vodacell. The limited data plans cost $\text{R120}$ for $\text{1}$ gigabyte (GB) per month, $\text{R135}$ for $\text{2}$ $\text{GB}$ per month and $\text{R150}$ for $\text{3}$ $\text{GB}$ per month. Assume this pattern continues indefinitely. Use a table to set up the pattern of the cost of the data plans. Find the general formula for the sequence. Use the general formula to determine the cost for a $\text{30}$ $\text{GB}$ data plan. The cost of an unlimited data plan is $\text{R520}$ per month. Determine the amount of data Raymond would have to use for it to be cheaper for him to sign up for the unlimited plan.
Make a table to see the pattern: Number of GB $(n)$ 1 2 3 4 Cost (in Rands) 120 135 150 165 Pattern 120 $120+(1)(15)=135$ $120+(2)(15)=150$ $120+(3)(15)=165$
Use the observed pattern to determine the general formula.: The price of $n$ GB of data is ${T}_{n}=120+15\left(n-1\right)$

Determine the cost of of data.: This question requires us to determine the value of the $30^{\text{th}}$ term, in other words, find ${T}_{n}$ if $n=30$ . Using the general formula, we get: $\begin{aligned}{T}_{n}&=120+15\left(n-1\right)\\\therefore{T}_{30}&=120+15\left(30-1\right)\\&=120+15\left(29\right)\\&=120+435\\&=555\end{aligned}$ Therefore the cost of a $\text{30}$ $\text{GB}$ data package is $\text{R555}$ .

Determine when it is cheaper to purchase the unlimited data plan: The final question of this worked example requires us to determine when it would be cheaper for Raymond to purchase an unlimited data plan instead of a limited plan. In other words, we need to find $n$ where $T_n$ is less than $\text{R520}$ . We know that: ${T}_{n}=120+15\left(n-1\right)$ Therefore, if $T_n=520=120+15\left(n-1\right)$ Solving for $n$ , we get: $\begin{aligned}520&=120+15\left(n-1\right)\\520&=120+15n-15\\520&=105+15n\\405&=15n\\\frac{405}{15}&=n\\n&=27\end{aligned}$ Therefore it is cheaper for Raymond to purchase the unlimited data plan if he uses more than $\text{27}$ $\text{GB}$ per month.

claims.claim: A sequence is an ordered list of items, usually numbers.
Each item which makes up a sequence is called a term.
The first term of a sequence is written T_1.
The fourth term of a sequence is written T_4.
The tenth term of a sequence is written T_10.
The general term is often expressed as the nth term and is written as T_n.
It is important to note the difference between n and T_n: n can be compared to a place holder indicating the position of the term in the sequence.
T_n is the value of the place held by n, so the position n and the value T_n are different things.
The common difference is the difference between any term and the term before it.
The common difference is denoted by d.
To calculate the common difference, find the difference between any term and the previous term.
For the sequence 10; 7; 4; 1, the common difference between the first two terms is found as d = T_2 - T_1 = 7 - 10 = -3.
Check the common difference with another two terms (for 10; 7; 4; 1, d = T_4 - T_3 = 1 - 4 = -3) and see that d is constant.
In general, the common difference is d = T_n - T_(n-1).
The common difference is the later term minus the earlier term, not the other way round: for example d = T_2 - T_1, not T_1 - T_2.
For 1; 4; 7; 10; ... there is a difference of 3 between successive terms, and the pattern is continued by adding 3 to the previous term.
For 13; 8; 3; -2; ... the difference is -5, and the pattern is continued by adding -5 to the previous term, which is the same as subtracting 5 from it.
Sequences with a common difference are called linear sequences.
To continue a figure pattern, make a table of the number of tables against the number of people seated to see if a pattern forms.
To describe a figure pattern, see how much the number of people increases for each table added (here 2 more each time, starting from 4), which gives the pattern 4; 6; 8; 10; ... and the next terms.
A sequence does not have to follow a pattern but, when it does, we can write down the general formula to calculate any term.
For the linear sequence 1; 3; 5; 7; 9; ... the nth term is given by the general formula T_n = 2n - 1.
To find a general formula, find the relationship between the position of a term and its value; the formula then matches the pattern and gives any term in the sequence.
To find the general formula for a list of terms such as 6; 1; -4; -9; ..., set the terms out in a table.
In the table for 6; 1; -4; -9; ..., the terms are written as 6 - 0x5, 6 - 1x5, 6 - 2x5, 6 - 3x5 and so the nth term is written as 6 - (n - 1) x 5.
The difference between the successive terms is always the coefficient of n in the formula; this is called a common difference.
For sequences with a common difference, the general formula will always be of the form T_n = dn + c, where d is the difference between each term and c is some constant.
For a picture pattern, make a table of the number of tables, n, against the number of people seated, and write the pattern for each term.
From the table (4 = 4+2(0), 6 = 4+2(1), 8 = 4+2(2), ...), the number of people seated at n tables is T_n = 4 + 2(n - 1).
There may be variations in how you think of a picture pattern; viewing the study table as 1 + 2n + 1 gives 2n + 2, and your formula for T_n will still be correct.
In the data plans table, the costs 135, 150, 165 are written as 120 plus 1, 2, 3 lots of 15, which is how the pattern is observed.
Use the observed pattern to determine the general formula: the price of n GB of data is T_n = 120 + 15(n - 1).
You can check a general formula by substituting values of n into the formula.
To calculate a required term, substitute its position for n in the general formula: for T_n = 4 + 2(n - 1), T_12 = 4 + 2(12 - 1) = 4 + 22 = 26.
To find how many tables are needed to seat 20 people, put T_n = 20 in the general formula and solve for n.
To solve for n, expand the brackets (20 = 4 + 2n - 2), collect the numbers (18 = 2n) and divide by the coefficient of n to get n = 9.
To determine the cost of a 30 GB plan, find T_n if n = 30, using the general formula.
Substituting n = 30 into T_n = 120 + 15(n - 1) gives T_30 = 120 + 15(29) = 555.
To find n when the value of a term is given, set T_n equal to that value (520 = 120 + 15(n - 1)), expand, simplify (520 = 105 + 15n, then 405 = 15n) and solve for n, giving n = 27.
From n = 27 the book concludes it is cheaper to purchase the unlimited data plan if he uses more than 27 GB per month.
